title: The 6 Skills You Need to Become a Strategic Leader
author: The Good Boss
summary: The author redefines strategic leadership away from the common notion of 'having a vision' and toward six specific, learnable skills illustrated with coaching anecdotes from his career as an engineering manager. Pattern recognition is the ability to see that separate small problems (missed deadlines, sick days) share a common root cause rather than treating each in isolation. Systems analysis means treating an organization as an interconnected web rather than siloed departments, so a decision in one team can have unseen effects elsewhere. Mental agility, structured problem-solving, visioning, and political savvy round out the list, each grounded in a specific failure or near-failure the author observed or experienced directly. The piece's overall claim is that these six skills, none of which appear on a resume or job posting, matter more for leadership effectiveness than the technical or soft skills that typically get trained and evaluated.
points: The central reframe — that strategic leadership is a bundle of six specific, coachable skills rather than 'having a vision' — pushes back on a common but vague leadership cliché with concrete, teachable practices.

The pattern-recognition example (two employees' missed deadlines and sick days traced to the same underlying legacy migration project) demonstrates how treating symptoms individually, rather than looking for shared causes, is a common managerial failure mode.

The Conway's Law reference — that a company's products end up mirroring how its teams communicate — gives systems analysis a concrete diagnostic test: silence between teams predicts disconnected products.

The claim that 'nothing goes exactly as planned' and that strategic leaders treat unexpected results as new information rather than a verdict on their competence reframes mental agility as an emotional discipline, not just a tactical skill.
quotes: Many managers think that strategic leadership is about "having a vision" and then driving towards that vision, but that's a very narrow way of looking at it.

That's what I call pattern recognition. It's the skill of noticing that seemingly separate, small events are actually interconnected or interrelated. Strategic leaders connect dots early, while everyone else is still looking at each incident individually.

Systems Analysis is about thinking of your organization as a spider's web instead of a stack of departments working in silos. When you pull on one strand in that hypothetical web, you will notice how they're interconnected.

That's mental agility: the ability to take a hit to the plan and adjust it, instead of digging in. The leaders who stay strategic are the ones who treat an unexpected result as new information, not a verdict on their own or their team's competence.

Political savvy isn't about manipulation. It's about understanding that your organization runs on people, and people have histories, incentives, and unwritten rules, whether you choose to learn them or not.
You've probably noticed this by now: none of the six skills I talked about in this post show up on your resume, or your LinkedIn profile.
